strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real pain points in 3D content creation where UV mapping is time-consuming and requires both technical precision and artistic judgment
Sound technical approach combining semantic awareness via Shape Diameter Function partitioning with visibility awareness via ambient occlusion in a principled differentiable framework
Comprehensive evaluation including comparisons against multiple strong baselines (FlexPara, Autodesk Maya, Blender SmartUV, xatlas) with both qualitative and quantitative metrics
Strong qualitative results clearly demonstrating improvements in seam placement in occluded regions and semantic alignment with 3D part structure across diverse mesh types
Thorough documentation and reproducibility: public code availability, detailed algorithm descriptions, extensive appendices, and clear mathematical formulations (Eqs. 1-8)

Thoughtful two-stage pipeline design that separates geometry-preserving learning from task-specific objectives, with clear loss function design including wrapping, cycle-consistency, anti-overlap, and distortion penalties
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (SDF partitioning from Shapira et al. 2008, ambient occlusion from Zhukov et al. 1998, bi-directional cycle mapping from recent work) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas

Quantitative improvements are often modest, particularly for geometry preservation metrics (conformality, equareality in Table 1) and semantic alignment metrics show only incremental gains over baselines

Absent user studies for validating perceptual quality claims—the core motivation about visibility is inherently perceptual, yet results are primarily visual inspection without psychophysical evaluation

Methodological concerns: soft seam membership scoring (Eq. 6) appears heuristic without sensitivity analysis; simple grid-based aggregation strategy lacks justification; SDF partitioning may fail on thin structures or complex topologies

Incomplete ablation studies—Table 5 ablates high-level objectives but lacks ablations on architectural choices, loss term weights, hyperparameter sensitivity, or comparison of alternative visibility proxies

Evaluation scope limitations: no dataset size/diversity reporting, missing computational cost analysis and runtime comparisons, no failure case analysis, no broader evaluation beyond external UV parameterization
Narrow scope focused specifically on UV mapping for mesh texturing with unclear applicability to other surface parameterization problems or broader geometry understanding tasks

Baseline concerns: FlexPara (2025) is very recent and not well-established; includes heuristic tools (Blender SmartUV) rather than purely learning-based comparisons; missing comparisons with other recent neural approaches

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing two perceptually important aspects of UV parameterization (semantic alignment and visibility-aware seam placement)
Comprehensive two-stage framework combining geometry-preserving learning with perceptual objectives
Extensive visual results across diverse mesh types demonstrating visually clean parameterizations
Detailed technical exposition with extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Interesting idea of using ambient occlusion as a proxy to guide seam placement toward less-visible regions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily combines existing techniques (bi-directional cycle mapping from Zhao et al. 2025, SDF partitioning from Shapira et al. 2008) with new loss functions, which is incremental
Misleading 'unsupervised' claim - the method requires careful engineering of five weighted loss terms with no explanation of how hyperparameters were selected or sensitivity analysis provided

Unfair baseline comparisons - primarily against general-purpose tools (Maya, Blender, xatlas) rather than specialized parameterization methods or other learning-based approaches designed for semantic-aware parameterization

Weak evaluation support for core claims - Table 5 shows semantic/visibility objectives cause only 'minor changes' in geometry metrics, and the paper provides no downstream validation that these objectives actually improve texture quality or usability

Unvalidated visibility-aware objective - using ambient occlusion as a visibility proxy is intuitive but unvalidated; no evaluation showing that seams in low-AO regions are actually less visible to users
Limited ablation studies - missing ablations on key components (sensitivity to loss weights, necessity of visibility objective, impact of grid aggregator design)
Insufficient evaluation scope - only simple organic shapes tested (animals, basic objects); no evaluation on complex CAD models, architectural geometry, or high-polygon meshes; small test dataset

No downstream validation - paper does not demonstrate that semantic-aware or visibility-aware parameterizations produce superior results for texture painting, synthesis, or other practical applications
Missing standard metrics and analysis - lacks quantitative evaluation of standard UV parameterization quality metrics, distortion distributions, seamlessness measures; no user studies
Ambiguous ground truth - semantic Hamming distance and Rand Index metrics require consistent semantic labeling, but methodology for consistent ground truth annotation across all meshes is unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real bottleneck in 3D content creation pipelines that currently requires significant manual effort
Novel dual-objective framework intelligently combining semantic-aware partitioning with visibility-aware seam placement, showing consistent practical improvements
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, diverse meshes, and multi-metric assessment (both qualitative and quantitative)
Solid technical execution with principled use of SDF for partitioning, differentiable soft seam membership for gradient flow, and bi-directional cycle mapping for geometric consistency
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-5) demonstrating the contribution of key components
Reproducible work with commitment to code release and detailed appendix explanations of methodology
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating method advantages over baselines
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty - primarily combines established techniques (SDF partitioning from Shapira et al. 2008, ambient occlusion standard in CG, cycle mapping from Zhao et al. 2025); architecture is engineering-focused rather than algorithmically innovative
Perceptual claims lack validation - no user study despite arguing that invisible seams are critical for quality; claimed benefits are not empirically validated with human subjects

No downstream task evaluation - paper motivates work for generative 3D models but provides zero evidence that improved UV parameterization enhances texture synthesis quality or other downstream applications

Modest quantitative improvements - Tables 1-2 show small magnitude gains (e.g., ~3% mean seam AO improvement), and Table 5 shows geometric metrics (conformality, equiareality) barely affected by adding semantic/visibility objectives
Incomplete semantic partitioning analysis - no validation that SDF-based partitions are semantically meaningful beyond visual inspection; no comparison to human-annotated ground truth labels
Methodological gaps - grid-based atlas aggregation acknowledged as simplistic but not compared to advanced solvers; multiple hyperparameters and loss weights mentioned without sensitivity analysis

Limited evaluation scope - tested only on simple organic objects; no evaluation on mechanical/CAD geometry, complex topologies, or scalability analysis; unclear generalization beyond demonstrated cases
Baseline comparison concerns - FlexPara and OptCuts training setup unclear; primary baselines include heuristic methods (Blender, xatlas); some recent learning-based methods not compared
Reproducibility gaps - network architecture partially specified; training data composition, hyperparameter values (λ weights), convergence criteria, and train/test splits not fully documented
Missing failure case analysis - no discussion of when/why method fails or performance on edge cases (symmetric objects, thin features, high-genus meshes)

strengths: Well-motivated semantic-aware and visibility-aware objectives that address genuine shortcomings in existing mesh parameterization methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including user study with 115 participants, comparisons against commercial tools and recent baselines, quantitative metrics, and thorough ablations
Fully unsupervised and end-to-end differentiable framework requiring no labeled training data
Strong empirical results with visibly better parameterizations and seams placed in less-noticeable regions compared to baselines
Practical significance for 3D content creation, addressing a real industry bottleneck confirmed by surveys
Code will be made publicly available, enhancing reproducibility
Clear presentation with informative figures and logical paper structure
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - individual components (bi-directional cycle mapping, Shape Diameter Function, ambient occlusion) are from existing work; novelty is primarily in combining them with two new loss terms, which feels incremental

Significant computational overhead: semantic-aware pipeline is much slower than FlexPara; visibility-aware pipeline incurs ~90% additional overhead due to AO computation and seam extraction, with insufficient cost-benefit analysis
Heavy dependence on initial mesh segmentation quality with limited discussion of failure modes, robustness to different shape types, or behavior when segmentation is poor
Visibility objective uses ambient occlusion as indirect proxy for perceptuality; doesn't account for varying lighting conditions or viewpoints; AO computation itself is expensive

Insufficient exploration of trade-offs between multiple objectives (Eq. 8); relative loss weights not thoroughly ablated; potential conflicts between distortion minimization and semantic/visibility objectives not deeply analyzed
Limited comparison with recent learning-based methods - only one recent neural baseline (FlexPara 2025); most comparisons are against traditional or commercial methods
User study limitations: 11 comparisons per participant, limited shape diversity, no evaluation under different lighting/rendering conditions
Missing ablations on loss hyperparameters, insufficient sensitivity analysis, and limited discussion of failure cases and when method underperforms
Scalability questions: most results on simple-to-moderate shapes; unclear performance on millions-of-triangle meshes; no explicit complexity scaling analysis
Seam visibility metric (mean AO of seam vertices) is indirect and indirect; lacks direct perceptual validation or strong correlation analysis with actual seam perceptibility
Dense presentation with critical implementation details in lengthy appendix (14+ pages); some design choices (soft seam membership, loss weights) not sufficiently justified
Concurrent nature of FlexPara comparison raises questions about fair evaluation and development timeline

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear real-world applicability in 3D content creation
Comprehensive evaluation including user study with 115 participants, ablation studies, and code released for reproducibility
Thoughtful combination of semantic-aware and visibility-aware objectives with clear intuitive appeal
Extensive technical documentation, detailed algorithmic descriptions, and well-organized appendices supporting reproducibility
Visual results demonstrate reasonable parameterizations with semantic parts well-aligned with UV charts
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily combines established techniques (ShDF from 2008, AO from 1998, cycle mapping from 2025) without substantial new algorithmic contributions

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares against FlexPara and OptCuts despite citing recent methods (Vermandere et al. 2024, Mukherjee et al. 2024, Cohen-Bar et al. 2025) without experimental validation against them
Indirect evaluation metrics: Hamming distance and Rand Index measure segmentation quality rather than UV parameterization quality; standard distortion metrics relegated to ablations
Computational cost prohibitive: visibility-aware variant requires ~60 minutes per mesh (Table 9), severely limiting practical applicability despite claimed benefits

Weak semantic partitioning justification: ShDF is a geometric heuristic; no evidence these partitions are semantically meaningful or comparison with learning-based semantic segmentation for mesh parts
Performance trade-offs not thoroughly investigated: Table 7 shows visibility-aware objective sometimes degrades conformality and equareality metrics while improving visibility
Ablation studies incomplete: missing comparison of base method without semantic/visibility objectives to isolate contribution of each component
Theoretical justification lacking: no formal analysis of why proposed objectives lead to quality UV maps; connection between objectives and parameterization quality is indirect

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing an important bottleneck in 3D content creation with novel semantic and visibility-aware objectives
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation including quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons against strong baselines (FlexPara, OptCuts), user study with 113 participants, and thorough ablations
Technically sound unsupervised framework that requires no labeled training data, enhancing generalization and practical deployment
Strong experimental results demonstrating improvements in both semantic alignment and seam visibility, with 74.29% expert preference for semantic-aware approach
Excellent reproducibility with detailed algorithmic descriptions, implementation details, public code release, and clear hyperparameter specifications
Novel technical contributions in soft seam membership scoring and AO-weighted seam loss that effectively combine geometric and perceptual objectives
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty - core bi-directional cycle mapping borrows heavily from Zhang et al. (2025) and Srinivasan et al. (2024), with main contribution being task adaptation

Significant computational overhead, particularly for visibility-aware pipeline (3640s vs 1250s for FlexPara, ~3x slower), limiting practical applicability despite paper's discussion of optimization opportunities
Semantic-visibility objective trade-off insufficiently analyzed - combined pipeline shows degraded conformality and no principled guidance provided for practitioners on weighting competing objectives
Semantic partitioning assumptions: SDF-based method requires specifying component count K and may not align with artist intentions; limited sensitivity analysis for K and SDF parameters

Limited experimental scope: evaluation on relatively simple geometric shapes (bunny, cow, fish) rather than complex real-world game/film assets; no challenging cases with fine details or non-convex geometry

User study design limitations: only 11 comparisons per participant from many possible methods, no evaluation of practical refinement workflows, and visual criteria may not capture all practitioner needs
Hyperparameter complexity with many loss weights and scaling factors (λ_wrap, λ_cycle, λ_repel, λ_ddi, λ_vis, λ_AO) and insufficient guidance for different application contexts
Visibility proxy limitations: ambient occlusion may not capture visibility under varied lighting conditions and connection to actual user perception of seam visibility is not empirically validated
Missing failure case analysis: no discussion of mesh types where method struggles, no examples of failure modes, unclear behavior on edge cases
Incremental contribution overall - while execution is solid, the work primarily adapts established architectures to a specific task with two novel loss objectives, offering modest conceptual advance
